articles.title: Amazon Burns Forty-Two Billion In Cash Chasing Cloud Growth
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAmazon reported earnings and revenue for the third quarter that missed Wall Street's expectations. The company held its 2026 capital expenditure forecast at $220 billion. Amazon's aggressive AI spending ate into its cash flow, with the company reporting an outflow of $42.4 billion. In this article Amazon shares plunged more than 6% in extended trading Thursday after the company reported disappointing third-quarter results and ballooning negative free cash flow, reflecting its swelling AI investments. Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: Wall Street was also looking at other key revenue numbers: The company held steady on its capital expenditure forecast for 2026, saying it continues to expect spending will reach $220 billion this year. Tech's hyperscalers have been on a blistering spending run to meet the surge in demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure, but signs have begun to emerge that the capex splurge is moderating. Earlier this week, Microsoft lowered its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, while Alphabet maintained its guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion. CEO Andy Jassy said on a conference call with investors that the company expects to "spend meaningfully more in 2027," and that Amazon has a "clear line of sight to attractive financial returns." The aggressive AI spending has eaten into Amazon's cash flow. The company posted negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, recording an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve month period, a swing of 386% year over year. In the prior quarter, the company reported negative free cash flow of $7.6 billion. The company said the shortfall was primarily due to an increase in purchases of property and equipment as a result of AI investments. Capital expenditures reached $77.3 billion during the quarter, ticking up from $35.1 billion one year earlier, and coming in well above analysts' estimated $58.7 billion, according to FactSet. Amazon said it expects fourth-quarter revenue to be in the range of $240 billion and $247 billion. The midpoint of its guidance was below Wall Street's expectations of $244.5 billion, according to LSEG. The fourth quarter is typically one of Amazon's biggest by revenue, due to the peak holiday shopping season. Sales in Amazon's cloud segment soared 39% year over year to $45.98 billion. That topped the consensus forecast for $45.29 billion and growth of 38%, according to StreetAccount. Jassy highlighted AWS acceleration in the earnings release, saying the company expects revenue growth rates of "over 40%" next year and in 2028. He added, "Our AWS investment in functionality and infrastructure is working." Jassy told investors on the call that he expects AWS will be a $1 trillion revenue business in the next five to 10 years. Amazon is facing pressure from Wall Street to show that its AI investments are lifting its revenues. The company pointed to growing traction for Bedrock, its AI model marketplace, along with its Trainium and Graviton AI chips. Jassy said Amazon's chips business "continues to grow triple-digit percentages year over year." He added that the company plans to make its Trainium chips available externally "late in 2027," assigning a timeframe to comments Jassy made earlier this year suggesting such a move. Third-quarter net income came in at $20.69 billion, or $1.89 per share, vs. $21.19 billion, or $1.95 per share, a year ago. The company said the decrease was driven primarily by a $9.5 billion pre-tax gain from its investment in the AI startup Anthropic, which was recorded in the 2025 third quarter. While the AWS segment continues to hum along, results weren't as bright in Amazon's retail business, which remains its largest unit by revenue, or its advertising segment. Online sales gained 2% year over year to $68.47 billion, which fell short of analysts' projected $69.68 billion, according to StreetAccount. It marked a slowdown from one year ago, when sales increased nearly 10%. Advertising revenue rose 11% year over year to $19.64 billion. That missed StreetAccount consensus estimates of $20.82 billion. Both units were impacted in part by Amazon's decision to pull its annual Prime Day sale forward in several countries from its typical third quarter timeframe into the second quarter so as to not conflict with the FIFA World Cup in July.
articles.summary: Amazon delivered its fastest cloud growth in nearly five years at 39%, yet the celebration ended there. Hyperscale capital spending drove free cash flow down to negative $42.4 billion, proving that maintaining AI parity requires bleeding cash faster than commercial software generates it. Andy Jassy is wagering enterprise balance sheets on accelerated compute before corporate software customers show sustained enterprise demand.

Gallagher, a former Republican member of the US Congress who led a House of Representatives committee focused on US strategic competition with China, said that Taiwan’s importance to AI development has grown to the point that Xi might need to act on Beijing’s designs toward the nation — especially in light of the competition between the US and China to dominate the technology. “The logic of Xi Jinping sacrificing enormously to take Taiwan is getting more compelling,” Gallagher said at a defense policy event in Indiana with US Senator Jim Banks. Chinese embassy in Washington spokesman Liu Chang (劉暢) said in a statement later on Wednesday that Beijing “brooks no external interference” and suggested the US “act prudently” on Taiwan. “The Taiwan question is China’s internal affair,” he said. “Stronger cooperation between enterprises on both sides of the Taiwan Strait in semiconductors and other fields is the right path toward mutual benefit and win-win outcomes.” As Taiwan is the home to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), it makes it a chokepoint that China could exploit to halt US progress in AI technology if authorities in Beijing found the US was gaining too much of a lead, Gallagher said. “If China takes Taiwan, they will control TSMC or disable TSMC — they will have the ability to hold the rest of the world economically hostage,” said Gallagher, who left Congress in early 2024 and joined Palantir later that year. While some prominent US officials have previously warned that China was seeking the capability to invade Taiwan by next year, the US has backed away from that projection, including in March with an intelligence assessment that concluded an invasion “would be extremely challenging and carry a high risk of failure.” Even so, China has stepped up patrols by its coast guard off Taiwan’s east coast, highlighting the risk that a blockade would pose to global supply chains in the event of a Chinese invasion. The patrols add to the regular military drills conducted by Chinese forces in the region. Palantir plays a critical role in the US military as a key provider of technology for the Pentagon, including its Maven Smart System, which uses AI for surveillance and targeting. articles.title: Utah State Regulators Hit Kalshi Founders with Criminal Gambling Charges
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets. Meanwhile, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed criminal charges in a state court against Kalshi and its founders on Wednesday. The attorney general’s office provided us with court filings listing charges against KalshiEX, LLC , Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour , and Kalshi co-founder and COO Luana Lopes Lara . The company and two co-founders each face 13 felony charges and one misdemeanor for violating gambling laws. The charges are based on sports bets offered on Kalshi between September 13 and September 24. “The state did not issue arrest warrants for Monsour and Lopes Lara. Instead, they have been issued summons to respond to the charges in Third District Court in Salt Lake County,” The Salt Lake Tribune wrote . The Utah News Dispatch quoted a Kalshi statement vowing to fight the charges. “This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” the statement said, referring to similar charges the company beat in Arizona in May. Utah, which prohibits gambling, filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events. “Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.” Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). Trump admin claims sole authority The CFTC “has filed a lawsuit against Utah to block the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets using state laws,” the commission said on Tuesday . “The lawsuit follows Utah’s decision to file civil enforcement actions in state court against CFTC-regulated markets and other businesses. Utah’s effort to restrict the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges obstructs Congress’s decision to federally preempt state law.” If Utah can shut down Kalshi, that could spell trouble for Kalshi’s chief prediction-market rival, Polymarket, and for sports betting sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. DraftKings and FanDuel advertise availability in all US states via a mix of products , including prediction-market platforms in states like Utah. Both are registered with the CFTC. The Utah attorney general’s office declined to comment today on the CFTC lawsuit. The CFTC previously filed lawsuits against Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin. The federal agency also filed briefs supporting Kalshi in appeals court cases. “Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets,” CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said. “Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes—they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets. As I’ve said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that’s exactly what we’ll do.” The US Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) gives the CFTC authority to regulate swaps. The key legal questions being grappled with by courts throughout the US are whether event contracts offered by prediction markets qualify as swaps, and whether the CFTC jurisdiction over swaps preempts states from applying their gambling laws. US sues in same court where Utah beat Kalshi The CFTC is suing Utah in the same US district court that previously ruled in Utah’s favor. Kalshi sued Utah in February in an attempt to stop the state from bringing an enforcement action against the prediction market. In August, US District Judge Robert Shelby granted Utah’s motion for summary judgment and denied Kalshi’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Shelby wrote , “[T]he court concludes the federal law relied upon by Kalshi does not preempt Utah’s ability to enforce its anti-gambling laws.” Shelby determined the text of US law makes it clear that state regulation is not forbidden. US law states that CFTC jurisdiction does not “supersede or limit the jurisdiction conferred on courts of the United States or any State,” and “explicitly provides for State regulation of its gaming laws in all but a few specified cases,” he wrote. “Congress is aware that some States permit gambling while others do not, and the CEA explicitly provides for State jurisdiction,” Shelby wrote. Most states in US want Supreme Court to rule Kalshi is now appealing its loss to the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit but was unable to obtain an injunction preventing enforcement of the state gambling ban while that litigation continues. On September 8, Tenth Circuit judges denied Kalshi’s emergency motion for an injunction pending appeal. Utah filed its lawsuit seeking a shutdown of Kalshi about six weeks later. The CFTC lawsuit against Utah makes arguments similar to the ones already rejected by the district court, although some other courts have ruled otherwise. “Utah is not the first State that has attempted to invade the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction over swaps,” the CFTC lawsuit said. “Already, several federal courts—including the Third Circuit—have swiftly responded by issuing or affirming temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions barring the States from enforcing their gambling laws against CFTC-regulated exchanges that offer sports-related or other event contracts.” The Third Circuit appeals court ruled that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. But Kalshi lost similar cases in the Sixth Circuit and Ninth Circuit in rulings that went in favor of Ohio, Tennessee, and Nevada. Because circuit appeals courts are divided on the issue, it is likely that the Supreme Court will take up the case and determine whether states can apply their gambling laws to prediction markets. New Jersey petitioned the Supreme Court to resolve the circuit split, and 39 other states and the District of Columbia filed a brief supporting New Jersey’s petition. This article was originally published on October 28 at 3:30 pm ET and updated on October 29 with information about the felony charges filed against Kalshi and its co-founders . articles.title: Amazon Artificial Intelligence Capex Crushes AWS Cloud Margin Gains
articles.content: Amazon’s cloud computing unit is growing steadily, keeping pace with AI demand, but the e-commerce giant’s massive spending on AI data centers and weaker advertising performance are worrying investors. Recommended Video Amazon on Thursday reported third-quarter revenue of $201.9 billion, slightly missing expectations. Its profit was $20.7 billion, which also fell short of expectations and was down from the same period a year ago. Amazon said the decline was due to gains it recorded a year earlier from its investment in AI company Anthropic. Amazon Web Services, the cloud unit, saw third-quarter sales rise 39.3% to $45.98 billion, topping Wall Street targets and marking its fastest growth in years. The results showed that demand for Amazon’s cloud services, particularly those tied to AI, remains high. But the Seattle-based company is also continuing to spend at unprecedented rates to keep up, and performance in its non-cloud businesses is weakening. On Thursday, Amazon said its quarterly capital expenditures totaled $75.9 billion and reiterated that it expects its 2026 capital spending to be about $220 billion. “This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy said in a call with analysts, defending the company’s capital spending. “What we’re seeing with AI, it’s the biggest transformation in our lifetime. We’re going to invest to continue being the leader.” Jassy said AWS should grow into a $1 trillion business in the next five to 10 years and that Amazon expects revenue growth in its cloud business to be 40% or more in 2027 and 2028. The forecast is unusually long-range for the company, but it signals confidence in future growth. The company’s advertising business grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, missing analyst expectations, and its projected holiday-quarter revenue and operating profit are below Wall Street estimates at the midpoint of the range. The heavy AI infrastructure spending also pushed its free cash flow deeply negative; the company said free cash flow swung from positive $14.8 billion to negative $42.4 billion over the past year. Amazon intends to begin selling its Trainium chips externally in late 2027. Jassy also predicted that 20% of all AI tokens consumed by enterprises over the next one to two years could be dedicated solely to security. Shares of the company sank more than 6% in after-hours trading. Amazon’s earnings came on the heels of those from peers such as Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet , which also reported robust growth in their cloud units and soaring AI infrastructure costs. Alphabet also reported weaker-than-expected advertising growth. The results have shown that the need for AI compute remains as high as ever, and so does the spending. Investors in Amazon and other tech giants are closely watching the tightrope that so-called hyperscalers are walking, and any sign of a slowdown scares those worried about a bubble popping. Amazon is one of the biggest spenders in building out data centers. The company, famous for opening hundreds of e-commerce warehouses around the U.S., has lately been putting its capital into AI hubs. Collectively, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms are expected to spend more than $700 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, mostly on data centers. For the current quarter, Amazon said it expects sales between $240 billion and $247 billion and operating income between $28.5 billion and $33.5 billion. The midpoints of both ranges are lower than what analysts predicted. Chief Financial Officer Brian Olsavsky said fuel and other transportation costs are expected to be higher in the fourth quarter than in the third. This year, Amazon held its annual Prime Day in the second quarter rather than the third, which affected third-quarter results. AI company Anthropic’s prospectus for its upcoming initial public offering, made public earlier this week, showed just how heavily the lab relies on Amazon and other major cloud companies for AI compute. Anthropic has committed to spending at least $110 billion on Amazon cloud services from this past May through April 2036, regardless of actual usage. That is part of Anthropic’s commitment of at least $389.9 billion in compute spending with companies including Microsoft, Alphabet, and SpaceXAI. According to Anthropic’s IPO filing, Amazon has invested about $18 billion in Anthropic and committed to invest up to another $15 billion. Because Amazon pioneered cloud computing, it’s growing off a larger customer base, so its growth rates can be lower than those of its peers. However, the AI boom has increased pressure on Amazon to show that its cloud unit is seeing as much demand as others, especially because Amazon’s spending is so high. Amazon has now entered its crucial holiday quarter, which generates most of its yearly revenue. The company recently said it plans to hire 300,000 workers for the holidays, a move it often makes to staff up as e-commerce demand peaks. Over the past three months, it has made a big hardware push, introducing Alexa tablets, the Bee AI wearable, and updated Echo products. Even as it hires for its warehouses, Amazon is cutting jobs elsewhere. This week it cut 250 jobs in its devices and services division, after earlier shedding about 1,000 people in its retail department. It laid off about 30,000 workers between late 2025 and early this year. The company is also evolving its AI strategy. In September, it blocked Meta’s popular new AI assistant , Muse, from accessing its online store. Muse is a threat to Amazon because it bypasses the usual process of humans visiting its website or app and seeing the advertisements that serve as a key profit driver. Jassy said Thursday that few customers are shopping through external agents because “the experience is still not great.” This week, Amazon told its software engineers in an internal memo, which it also published in a blog, that they should embrace AI but will ultimately be judged on outcomes, not on how many tokens they consume or how much code they generate. “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the company said. “Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions. An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.” Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. articles.title: Autonomous Drones Attack Commercial Shipping Vessel In Black Sea
articles.content: Three maritime drones struck a container ship sailing in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria on Wednesday, the country’s defense minister said, the latest in a string of such incidents on NATO’s eastern flank. The attack on the Liberian-flagged container ship, the Contship Jet, occurred a little before 1 p.m. local time about 21 nautical miles southeast of the coastal town of Shabla, near Cape Kaliakra in northeastern Bulgaria, Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters. The crew evacuated the vessel and were eventually taken on board rescue vessels of the Bulgarian Navy and border police, according to the state news agency BTA. The rescued sailors — 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians — were being transported to the port city of Varna for medical checks. The ship was en route from Israel’s port of Haifa to Constanța in Romania. It was not immediately clear what the 421 containers on board were carrying. The incident took place as defense ministers from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey were meeting in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, for trilateral talks focused on security in the Black Sea region. In a statement after the talks, the three NATO countries strongly condemned the drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and called for an “immediate cessation of attacks that threaten commercial ships, maritime infrastructure and the safety of maritime activities.” They also agreed on stronger intelligence sharing, early warning capabilities and coordination in the Black Sea. A series of drone attacks have occurred this month off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, leading some members of the alliance to wonder if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Russia has not taken responsibility for the attacks, but suspicion has fallen on Moscow . Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country’s Parliament earlier this month that “the logic points in that direction … The problem is that we cannot prove it.” On Oct. 15, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that NATO had “strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities” in the face of increasingly frequent strikes on commercial vessels. The attacks in Bulgaria and Romania’s exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube River ports, leaving Kyiv increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine’s Danube ports. In early October, two commercial ships were attacked in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, and a week later, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity sank after being struck about 17 nautical miles east of Shabla while the Malta-flagged Chelsea 3 was damaged in a separate attack about 17 nautical miles east of Byala, according to reports at the time. On Oct. 23, a foreign-flagged cargo ship capsized and sank in the Black Sea following a suspected drone strike about 13 nautical miles off the Romanian port city of Constanta. articles.title: Congressional Leaders Demand Preservation of Executive Branch AI Chatbot Records
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By Grace Dille , Technology Reporter, Nextgov/FCW | October 29, 2026 12:17 PM ET The request to preserve AI conversations could signal what's to come if Democrats flip the House in next week’s election. White House Congress Records Management The top Democrats on the House Judiciary and Oversight panels are calling on President Donald Trump to preserve his conversations with artificial intelligence chatbots, including billionaire Elon Musk’s Grok. Reps. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., and Robert Garcia, D-Calif., sent a letter to Trump on Wednesday demanding that the White House preserve “any prompts” that the president or his staff have submitted to AI chatbots such as Grok, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Perplexity. They also said the White House must preserve any AI-generated outputs in response to those prompts. The lawmakers said their request “is not optional,” noting that the Presidential Records Act requires the adequate documentation of presidential records. “Preserving the President’s and his advisors’ AI prompts is thus essential to preserving an accurate historical record and informing future administrations against the gaping national security vulnerabilities created by this Administration’s apparent reliance on unsecured, privately operated AI systems,” they wrote. Raskin and Garcia are also requesting a closed-door briefing with the president and his staff by Nov. 11 on their use of AI chatbot technologies. The lawmakers said their request is informed by reporting from Time that said Trump “sought the chatbot’s advice on carrying out some of your presidential duties, including asking Grok to opine on how Venezuelans would respond to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro.” Weeks later, the lawmakers said, Trump “ordered the U.S. military, without congressional authorization, to attack Venezuela and capture President Maduro.” They added that Trump “reportedly ‘came away thinking Grok was ingenious.’” The top Democrats called the episode “deeply troubling” because Trump allegedly consulted a chatbot, not Congress, on military operations. They also said the unsecured use of AI chatbots exposes the United States to national security risks and “malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties.” The lawmakers are requesting details on the White House’s document retention policies governing AI-generated materials, AI chatbot contracts, Trump’s use of AI chatbots, and cybersecurity safeguards applied to AI chatbot usage. "The White House preserves all required records in accordance with the law," a White House official told Nextgov/FCW. articles.content: Artificial intelligence is one of the economic sectors where the EU and China could be allies rather than foes; both are racing to close the gap with the United States. But until now, the EU has viewed China as a competitor and threat on AI and digital technology.  The two economies “have huge cooperation potential in new energy, AI, services trade, the digital economy and green low-carbon fields”, China’s ministry of commerce said in a statement following the second round of China-EU trade talks in Beijing earlier this month.  Those two days of talks between EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and Chinese commerce secretary Wang Wentao were widely viewed as a successful first step forward by EU leaders at last week’s summit in Brussels.   In particular, China has agreed to reduce exports of electric vehicles and guarantees continued access to rare earths without new export controls. It also commits EU and Chinese officials to at least six more months of negotiations on a raft of trade disputes.  A visit to a robotics factory was part of the itinerary for a delegation from the European Parliament’s international trade committee who will make a three day visit to China from 27 October.  Committee chairman Bernd Lange told reporters that Unitree Robotics, a Chinese robotics company that uses its own humanoid robots—powered by embodied AI —to help manufacture and assemble more robots would be “at the heart of Chinese industry in the future.”  China is the world leader in the robotics market, with Lange’s Germany its main European rival.  To read this story, log in or subscribe Enjoy access to all articles and 25 years of archives, comment and gift articles. articles.title: Voter Backlash Targets Data Center Grids Across American Electoral Campaigns
articles.content: By Anna Lieb The U.S. data center boom is emerging as a key issue in political advertising on social media in the home stretch of the midterm campaign season, a Pew Research Center analysis finds. Spending on political ads mentioning data centers has increased exponentially in the run-up to the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Over a period of 90 days from Jul. 27 to Oct. 24, advertisers on Facebook and Instagram spent almost $12 million on ads that mention data centers in the context of social issues, elections or politics. (In this analysis, we refer to these ads as “political ads.”) As recently as January, pro-data center sentiment was slightly more common in this advertising than anti-data center sentiment. Among political ads mentioning data centers, 42% were supportive of them while 31% were critical. The remainder did not take a clear stance. But since the beginning of this year, ads that mention data centers have grown increasingly critical. So far in October, 57% of these ads have expressed opposition to data centers, while just 3% have been clearly in favor of them. This finding comes as Americans’ views of data centers have grown more negative in recent months. This Pew Research Center analysis looks at U.S. political ads on Facebook and Instagram that discuss data centers. Pew Research Center does research to help the public, media and decision-makers understand important topics. This research builds on our recent work about data centers and artificial intelligence. Learn more about Pew Research Center and our work on artificial intelligence. Facebook and Instagram advertising data comes from the Meta Ad Library API. The Ad Library is maintained by Meta and includes every advertisement about politics, elections or social issues appearing on Meta platforms worldwide. For simplicity, we use “political ads” throughout this post to refer to these ads. For this analysis, we identified every ad in the Ad Library that mentioned data centers in its text or audio and ran on Facebook or Instagram in the United States from Jan. 1 to Oct. 24, 2026. Most of the ads we identified (87%) ran on both platforms. For each ad, we collected its text, the states in which it ran and how much was spent to run it. Meta provides ad spending data as a range, so we used the midpoint of each ad spend range when calculating total spending. We then used GPT-5.6 Luna to determine if each ad: Across all of these categories, the model achieved an average F1 score of 0.88 and 95% accuracy on a validation dataset of 300 ads coded by trained human coders. See the full model prompt we used to classify these ads. We also used several other data sources to complement this analysis. These include historical data on total political ad spending from the Meta Ad Library Report as of Oct. 24; the number of competitive House, Senate and gubernatorial races in each state, according to the Cook Political Report on Oct. 24; and the number of current and planned data centers in each state based on Data Center Map estimates on Oct. 27. Some common themes emerge in political ads on Facebook and Instagram that mention data centers: Certain themes are more common in ads that are critical of data centers than in ads that support them. For example, nearly half of ads that oppose data centers discuss the corporate interests behind them, like the tech industry or utility companies. That is roughly double the share of pro-data center ads that mention these interests. Meanwhile, ads that support data centers disproportionately discuss their impact on jobs. A majority (61%) of recent spending on Facebook and Instagram political ads about data centers has been on ads that don’t promote specific candidates for office. These ads are typically paid for by advocacy groups. More than half of these ads (56%) express opposition to data centers, but 13% are supportive – a much larger share than among campaign ads. The remaining 39% of recent spending has been for ads that support specific candidates. Of the campaign ads in our analysis period, 72% promote Democratic candidates and 15% promote Republican candidates, while the remainder are for independent candidates or those whose party affiliation could not be determined. A majority of these campaign ads are critical of data centers, and this holds true across party lines. Pro-data center ads are rare for both parties, occurring in less than 1% of campaign ads overall. In other words, Democratic candidates are more likely than Republicans to post political ads about data centers. But when they do talk about data centers, Democratic and Republican candidates are similarly critical of them. Since late July, advertisers spent more than $1 million on political ads mentioning data centers that targeted Facebook and Instagram users in each of three states – Ohio, Wisconsin and Texas. Data center ads made up about 14% of all the political ad spending on these platforms that was aimed at users in Wisconsin, the highest share of any state. In general, states with more competitive elections for the U.S. House of Representatives, Senate or governor have seen more spending on Facebook and Instagram political ads about data centers. Spending on these ads is also higher, on average, in states with more operational or planned data centers. is a computational social science analyst at Pew Research Center.

articles.title: Pentagon Investigates Cyberattack Compromising Military Base Cold Chains
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By David DiMolfetta , Cybersecurity Reporter, Nextgov/FCW | October 29, 2026 04:54 PM ET August outages spoiled food at military commissaries across the nation. Investigators are also examining a similar attack on refrigeration systems in France. Defense Cyber Threats International The Pentagon is investigating a suspected cyberattack behind freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the United States in August, according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter. The outages affected some six commissaries — the on-base grocery stores serving military personnel — per the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the situation. At Fort Huachuca in Arizona, officials reported that a freezer had entered defrost mode and heated its contents, leaving food spoiled. Reuters first reported Thursday that investigators were treating the incidents as a possible hack. It’s unclear who might be responsible or whether investigators have conclusively determined what caused the failures. Cyber Command and various Defense Department law enforcement units are probing the incident. French authorities are also working with officials examining the matter. Earlier this month, hackers overrode temperature controls on commercial refrigeration equipment at more than 350 French establishments, forcing supermarkets to discard spoiled food. The investigation draws attention to the computers that control everyday equipment used to store and handle food, an often overlooked area of cybersecurity where a hack can spoil supplies or interrupt distribution of goods. The unusual U.S. outages and the possibility of hacking were initially flagged in August by the Signal and Silence blog . Stars and Stripes subsequently reported the involvement of military investigators, and The Telegraph also reported officials’ contact with French authorities. A 2021 DHS assessment of threats to food and agriculture specifically identified refrigeration failures and shipping delays as cybersecurity risks that could cause spoilage and shortages. The Food and Agriculture Information Sharing and Analysis Center, an industry group that shares cyber threat intelligence on the nation's food supply, has warned that attackers are targeting internet-accessible industrial controls that may not have optimal cyberdefenses in place. The agri-food sector’s sensitivity to downtime often gives ransomware groups leverage to demand payment, the organization said in a separate report . Lawmakers have sought to improve federal protections. A bipartisan group reintroduced the Farm and Food Cybersecurity Act in 2025, following an earlier proposal introduced in 2024. Share This:

articles.title: Federal Law Enforcement Seizes Bulletproof Hosting Giant Virtualine Domain
articles.content: Authorities seized the domain of Virtualine , a bulletproof hosting provider that cybercriminals used to commit a large-scale sextortion scheme, ransomware, data theft, malware hosting and money laundering, the Justice Department said Tuesday.  Virtualine facilitated prolific criminal activity, including the distribution of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), the Justice Department said. The Russian-speaking bulletproof hosting provider was among the most active this year in crypto-related crime in particular, researchers said.  The site and its associated infrastructure stands out among the dozens of bulletproof hosting providers currently tracked by TRM Labs. “It was not among the largest by total inflows, but it received the most illicit-attributed value in 2026 to date,” the blockchain and cryptocrime research firm wrote in a blog post . Virtualine received almost one-fifth of all illicit-attributed inflow among bulletproof hosting providers tracked by TRM this year to date. A Russian drug marketplace accounted for nearly 44% of the direct payments Virtualine received from customers and attributed counterparties so far this year, according to TRM. A sextortion scheme accounted for nearly 17% of direct payments to Virtualine, followed by a cryptocurrency mixer at almost 13%, ransomware at nearly 5%, cybercrime services at 3% and malware at 2%. “Virtualine is another example of Russia’s illicit economy at work: darknet markets, ransomware groups, non-compliant exchanges, and brokers all feeding the same ecosystem,” Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, said in a prepared statement.  “Bulletproof hosting is the connective tissue. Seizing a domain matters, but the blockchain record doesn’t disappear with it. It shows who is paying, who is getting paid, and where they go next,” he added.  Virtualine attracted many criminals as customers. Ransomware groups, including Coinbase Cartel, The Gentlemen, INC, DragonForce and Qilin all paid the site’s operators, according to TRM. The bulletproof hosting provider also received payments from the StealC infostealer, the Matanbuchu loader, bot and malware-distribution services and sites linked to CSAM.  The FBI and prosecutors got a court order to seize Virtualine’s primary domain, which was also known as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo and Omegatech. Officials said Virtualine continued hosting services for a customer that distributed CSAM and a hack-for-hire service after it received numerous notices from law enforcement in Germany, Canada, Australia, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children and a victim’s attorney. TRM underscores that Virtualine was disrupted, but not completely shut down. “A domain seizure disrupts how customers find and access a service,” researchers wrote. “It does not, by itself, establish that the operator has stopped working, or that customers have lost access to all underlying infrastructure.”

articles.title: China Classified Reusable Spaceplane Expands Autonomous Orbital Operations
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military’s X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image. The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force. The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space. Lower-resolution views of a Chinese spaceplane showing the vehicle’s general shape were publicly available before the Defense Intelligence Agency assessment. A US Space Force official revealed Maxar’s observation at a 2024 conference in South Korea, but the Pentagon did not release the full-resolution image to the public until Monday, when it appeared in an unclassified DIA assessment of threats to the United States in space. Catch and Release The DIA report doesn’t reveal much new about what the Chinese spaceplane does in orbit. China has launched four spaceplane missions since 2020, with durations of up to nine months. The fourth mission is in orbit today after launching in February. It is not publicly known whether China has one or more such spaceplanes in its inventory. The Space Force has two X-37Bs flying in rotation, with the longest of their eight missions to date running two-and-a-half years from launch until landing. US officials have released photos of the X-37B vehicles, published information about their design and dimensions, and disclosed a handful of experiments they have carried into orbit. Most of the X-37B’s activities in space are classified. Like the X-37B, China’s spaceplane lifts off inside the payload shroud of a conventional rocket, then operates as a satellite once in orbit. The spaceplane flies like a miniature unpiloted version of NASA’s Space Shuttle and reenters the atmosphere for an autonomous land runway landing at the end of each mission. Ground teams then refurbish it for another flight. The “enhanced maneuverability” of spaceplanes makes them “more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA said in its report. So far, the Chinese spaceplane has only flown in low-Earth orbit (LEO) at an altitude of a few hundred miles. One of the Space Force’s X-37B flights soared to an altitude of more than 24,000 miles before using aerobraking to set up for reentry and landing . from their cargo bay. Most recently, China demonstrated an ability to catch an object in orbit, perhaps using a robotic arm. The vehicle now in space released a sub-satellite in June and recaptured it in July, then did the same thing again in August and September, according to an analysis of open source orbital tracking data by Jonathan McDowell , an astrophysicist who catalogs spaceflight activity. A Fleeting Glance The official name of the Chinese spaceplane is even a mystery. It is often called Shenlong in Western publications, citing reports from the 2000s about China’s development of a robotic spaceplane. Chinese state media only refer to the vehicle as Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, or CSSHQ, which means reusable experimental spacecraft, according to a fact sheet published by the Secure World Foundation . The DIA did not disclose the exact circumstances of Maxar’s observation of the Chinese spaceplane, such as its timing, location, or distance, but Earth observations often use cameras to view other objects in space as their orbits intersect, an emerging field known as non-Earth imaging (NEI). NEI allows commercial operators and government analysts to inspect satellites. This is especially useful for gleaning information about classified or proprietary satellite designs, extending a new avenue for international and corporate espionage to the high frontier. The capability exhibited by Maxar and other commercial companies in the NEI field is distinct from the recent actions of some military spacecraft, such as Russia’s Kosmos 2612, which deliberately maneuvered to approach a US-registered radar imaging satellite earlier this month. Commercial NEI observations come from chance encounters, often at extremely high speed. Pew-Pew With DEWs The DIA’s assessment of space threats includes an update on China’s pursuit of anti-satellite technology, or “counterspace” weapons. The intelligence agency reported the Chinese military likely considers directed-energy weapons (DEWs) “ideal counterspace systems” because they can be used to permanently or temporarily disable a satellite.
